Using the properties of addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors to isolate the $j$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1{a}_{1}+j{a}_{2} & =0 \\ 1\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}+j\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ j\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-1\begin{bmatrix}-6 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\ j\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the first components, we get

$$
2j=6\,⟹\,j=3.
$$

But then

$$
\begin{aligned}3\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\ne \begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, there is no $j$ such that $1{a}_{1}+j{a}_{2}=0.$
